newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus march disperses after clash with police.
newsitem.headline: Belarus march disperses after clash with police.

text.p: Belarus police, banging truncheons menacingly against riot shields, clashed in Minsk on Sunday with demonstrators protesting against a referendum next week in which President Alexander Lukashenko will seek to extend his term.
Eyewitnesses said several people were slightly hurt, but there were no reports of serious injuries.
The demonstrators, who carried white and red Belarussian tricolour flags, dispersed from the so-called "March of Silence" after several hours.
But parliamentary deputies urged them to return at 2 p.m. (1200 GMT) on Monday when parliament is to meet in emergency session to debate the political situation in the former Soviet republic.

The demonstrators say Lukashenko is seeking dictatorial powers. He says his presidency is a crusade against corruption in the country of 10 million and he has vowed to dismiss anyone who does not recognise the vote.

The march, which brought a turnout of between 5,000 and 10,000 people, was the latest in a series of protests against Lukashenko's proposals, which would allow him to extend his term in office by two years without a new election.
"Long live Belarus," the marchers chanted. Among themselves, they grumbled about Lukashenko's efforts to create a union with neighbouring Russia.

Some marchers wore cloth gags to symbolise the way the Belarussian media has covered previous similar protests. Local radio made no mention of the march, but continued its relentless drive to encourage people to turn out and vote.
The referendum officially takes place next Sunday, but polling stations are already open.
Lukashenko sent all voters a colour postcard of himself on Saturday and urged them to vote.
"Mafia clans and the owners of ill-gotten capital have united against the president you elected," Lukashenko wrote on the card, which showed him standing hand on heart in front of an adoring crowd.
"I turn to you, the honest people, to help save the country for the sake of our common future."
His supporters said people should vote before November 24, when questions drafted by parliament will also be on the ballot paper.
Some deputies have been staying in parliament around the clock because they fear the president will close the building.
Their supporters have been picketing the building and deputies called the emergency session for Monday.
Opposition deputies have said they would start impeachment proceedings against the president, although it is not clear if this will be on the agenda at Monday's session.
"I was beaten with a truncheon," Stanislav Bogdankevich leader of the United Civic party and parliamentary opposition told a news conference.
"They taught me a lesson for agreeing with Lukashenko," he said ironically, referring to his former central bank post.
Lukashenko has already shown that he will brook no opposition to his rule. On Thursday he sacked the head of the electoral commission which monitors voting in the republic.
He has banned independent trade unions, sacked newspaper editors and closed radio stations. He threatened this week to expel two Russian television journalists.
Communists, liberals and nationalists have joined forces to oppose the president's authoritarian style, but there is no strong or united opposition and no independent media.
